items.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
items.summary:
• Management team were in line for huge payouts

  • Fifa denies Infantino would have profited from plan

Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.

Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century.

Continue reading...
items.t: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show

items.title: WSL talking points: Captain Spence inspires Spurs shock win at City and Lionesses impress
items.summary:
We may have a proper title race on our hands as City and Chelsea drop points and LCL strengthen their grip on third place

Drew Spence rolled back the years with a vintage performance as her Tottenham side produced a shock 3-1 victory away against the defending champions, Manchester City. The 34-year-old marshalled the midfield and then had the vision to thread an outstanding through ball that split the City defence and found the run of Matilda Vinberg, who put Spurs 2-1 up. “She’s unbelievable. There are so many more gears in Drew and I wish I’d been able to work with her a bit earlier [in my career] because her leadership is second to none,” the Tottenham head coach, Martin Ho, said of the club captain. “Her performance levels, since I’ve been here, week on week have grown. She is covering every blade of grass and leads by example. For me, she’s one of the best midfielders in the league.” Tom Garry

Match report: Manchester City 1-3 Tottenham

items.t: WSL talking points: Captain Spence inspires Spurs shock win at City and Lionesses impress

items.title: Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’
items.summary:
The US-led four-country bid will be confirmed in Zurich on Monday, projecting record-setting total revenues of $4bn

The biggest and most lucrative event in the history of women’s sport will be confirmed at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress in Zurich on Monday, with a joint bid from the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031’s Women’s World Cup to be formally ratified by a vote of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

In the bid book submitted to Fifa last year the prospective hosts pledged to generate total revenues of $4bn if awarded hosting rights, which would represent a staggering increase on the $570m earnings from the last World Cup held in Australia and New Zealand three years ago, the first women’s tournament to break even.

items.t: Inside Fifa and US Soccer’s plan for 2031 World Cup: ‘the largest women’s sporting event in history’

The Baltimore Ravens have lost in all sorts of fashion in recent weeks. There were the blowout losses to juggernauts Buffalo, Jacksonville, and Cincinnati. items.title: England and Ireland provide champagne rugby for north to tee up finals weekend | Robert Kitson
items.summary:
France have the chance to topple the Springboks in the Nations Championship decider, with their Six Nations rivals also shining this autumn

Even if the official November Test window had now closed, as used to be the case, this would already have been a vintage European autumn. Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday.

Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka. A record-breaking 37-12 home win was then swiftly followed by Ireland defeating the world champion Springboks 20-17 to complete another resounding northern hemisphere double whammy.

items.title: ‘Haaland must be worried’: Thierno Barry’s rise has David Moyes purring
items.summary:
Everton striker has worked hard to find his scoring touch after admitting he hit ‘rock bottom’ at times last season

A most unexpected name sits behind the phenomenon Erling Haaland and the £125m proven marksman Alexander Isak in the Premier League goalscoring chart this season. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the refusal to quit.

“Fabulous” was David Moyes’s take on Barry’s last performance for Everton, when a double against Coventry took the striker to 10 goals for the season in all competitions and his team temporarily up to fifth. It was high praise indeed from a manager who does not dispense tributes freely, and can appear to be on the French forward’s case constantly, but was no more than Barry deserved for a display that also featured an assist for Everton’s third goal of the night. His six Premier League goals leave him joint third alongside Evanilson of Bournemouth and Aston Villa’s Nicolas Jackson.

items.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
items.summary:
Leeds offer Chelsea a lesson, Newcastle’s summer recruits struggle and Jules Ahoka makes a name for himself

What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. Leny Yoro’s very early red card may have been questionable but for the wall to evaporate and allow Dominik Szoboszlai’s subsequent free-kick to arrow home was damning evidence of how immature Pochettino’s new charges are. From here it became a debacle and the players, if they have anything about them, need to apologise to the head coach, hold a meeting between themselves and demand they start taking responsibility. If not, United are heading only one way: down. Jamie Jackson

Match report: Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United

items.summary:
• Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday

  • Uzbek challenger enters as the oddsmakers’ favorite

  • Champion plays down slump after falling to No 26

  • Read our World Chess Championship watch guide

World chess champion Gukesh Dommaraju insisted he was approaching his first title defense with the mindset of a challenger on Sunday as he and Javokhir Sindarov faced the media ahead of their historic showdown in Geneva, the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title.

The two 20-year-old grandmasters appeared side by side at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva, where they struck a respectful tone before their best-of-14-games encounter begins on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva.

items.summary:
• Price beats Gian van Veen 16-11 to secure title

  • Welshman lost ‘so many finals’ in four years of pain

Gerwyn Price finally ended his major trophy drought by winning the Grand Slam of Darts and is delighted to silence his critics. The Welshman had not won a major televised event since 2022 and may have thought it might not happen again after losing three finals this year alone.

But with Luke Littler and Luke Humphries exiting early, Price took his chance with a brilliant 16-11 win over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton. Price claimed Grand Slam glory for the fourth time, but this one will surely mean the most to him.

items.title: Alcaraz puts Zverev in shade as world’s best beats No 1 for first ATP Finals title
items.summary:
• Spaniard wins final 6-2, 7-6 (7) against new world No 1

  • Alcaraz the fourth to win career grand slam and ATP Finals

The titles of ATP world No 1 and the best male tennis player in the world are carried by two different names. This has always been clear throughout this messy, injury-ravaged men’s season but it was underlined in the grand finale as Carlos Alcaraz ended his campaign with a statement victory, defeating the top-ranked player, Alexander Zverev, 6-2, 7-6 (7) to win the ATP Finals for the first time.

So much of Alcaraz’s fortunes this season were defined by the wrist injury that forced him out for four and a half months during the spring and summer. No matter, he still managed to tick the two most important items off his to-do list this year.

items.title: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer
items.summary:
• Harlequins 21-48 Bristol

  • Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club

As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope and she was dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her Bristol debut. The full-back did it under significant pressure too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener.

The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old, and if her debut is anything to go by he will be proved right. The World Cup winner not only scored two tries but was also a linchpin in Bristol’s attack. Her gamechanging reputation was felt among her former teammates as she drew multiple defenders to her whenever she had the ball, meaning the wings on her outside had a lot more joy. The back three looked formidable with both wings, Reneeqa Bonner and Millie David, also scoring two tries apiece.

Continue reading...
items.t: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer

items.title: Tyson Fury looks back: ‘Once the Anthony Joshua fight is over, what will I do next? Walking the dog ain’t gonna cut it’
items.summary:
The former heavyweight boxing champion on falling in love at first sight, being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and the much-anticipated match

Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.

This was taken when I was nine, back when I was cute, shy and poorly dressed. The jumper would have been knitted by my grandma. The hairstyle isn’t great but a lot better than what I have now. I loved boxing and I loved singing.

items.title: England’s strength in depth finally comes together in landmark victory over All Blacks | Andy Bull
items.summary:
Record-breaking win suggests Steve Borthwick’s side are realising their enormous potential at last

Something’s coming. Oh yes. They will be able to hear its approaching footsteps in Edinburgh and Dublin and Paris and Cardiff, the tremors will ripple through Johannesburg and Sydney all the way to Auckland, where they will finally arrive sometime when the New Zealand public wakes up to find out all about what happened to their team here at Twickenham. After years of being oh so ordinary, England are on their way at long last to looking like the sort of team their depth of talent and wealth of resources has always suggested they ought to be.

When they beat Australia, everyone said how woeful the Wallabies were, when they thrashed Japan, all the talk was about how far the Brave Blossoms had fallen, but there are no caveats when you beat New Zealand like this. There’s no such thing as an easy win against the All Blacks. And no such thing, either, as a bad All Blacks team, even if this one’s a long way short of their best. It was a record victory, the 25-point margin eight more than England managed to win by in their famous victory here in 2012. Honestly, it could, maybe should, have been by more. England had…
items.t: England’s strength in depth finally comes together in landmark victory over All Blacks | Andy Bull
